nameStory: The lilac-brown bolete gets its name from its distinctive coloring that blends purplish-lilac tones with rich chocolate brown hues. This beautiful color combination makes it stand out among other boletes, especially when the cap catches the light filtering through the forest canopy.
description: The lilac-brown bolete is a medium-sized mushroom with a distinctive dark purple to chocolate brown cap that feels smooth to the touch. Instead of gills, it has tiny pores on the underside of its cap, making it a member of the bolete family. The stem is covered in fine scales and the whole mushroom has an elegant, sturdy appearance. This species forms beneficial partnerships with tree roots, helping forests stay healthy.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Smooth, velvety cap ranging from dark purple to rich chocolate brown, often with lilac undertones that shimmer in sunlight

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Tiny pores instead of gills on the cap underside, colored chocolate to violet-brown, like looking at coffee grounds through a magnifying glass

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Covered in fine scales that feel slightly rough when you run your finger along it, giving it a textured appearance

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Produces a reddish-brown spore print when the cap is placed gill-side down on white paper overnight

idTips.label: Safety Note
idTips.description: Once considered edible but now linked to severe stomach illness - never eat wild mushrooms without expert identification

habitat: Look for lilac-brown boletes in mixed forests throughout New England, where they grow near both coniferous trees like pine and hemlock, and deciduous trees like oak and maple. They prefer well-drained forest soils with good leaf litter and are often found along forest edges or in clearings. This species forms mycorrhizal relationships with tree roots, so you'll always find them near living trees rather than on rotting logs.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in spring, though warmer late spring rains may trigger early fruiting in southern New England forests.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for lilac-brown boletes, especially after warm summer rains when humidity is high and soil moisture is abundant.
seasonality.fall: Continue fruiting into early fall, often producing their most colorful specimens when temperatures begin to cool but soil stays warm.
seasonality.winter: Not active during winter months, existing underground as mycelia connected to tree roots.

funFact: This mushroom was such a taxonomic puzzle that scientists created an entirely new genus just for it! DNA analysis revealed it didn't truly belong with any existing bolete groups, despite looking similar to several other genera.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other dark-capped boletes, but the combination of smooth cap, scaly stem, and distinctive lilac-brown coloring helps distinguish it. Remember: 'Lilac sheen, scaly stem' - if you see both features together, you've likely found your lilac-brown bolete.
contextualKnowledge: This species has bounced between three different scientific genera (Boletus, Leccinum, and Tylopilus) before finally getting its own genus, Sutorius, showing how molecular genetics has revolutionized mushroom classification in recent decades.
compareHints: As the only Sutorius species in New England, compare it to other dark boletes in the Boletaceae family. Unlike Tylopilus species which have pink spore prints, the lilac-brown bolete has a reddish-brown spore print. Unlike Leccinum boletes which have prominent black scabers on white stems, this species has fine scales on a darker stem background.
